              NRG ENERGY, INC.’S COMMENTS ON STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT
        NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in this project on
the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) Staff’s discussion draft 1 regarding large load
interconnection standards to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) 2 § 37.0561 adopted by
the Texas Legislature through Senate Bill 6 (SB6) in the 89th Legislative Session. 3 NRG is the parent
company of well-established retail electric providers (REPs) and power generation companies (PGCs)
in the competitive electricity markets in Texas.
                                                   INTRODUCTION

        NRG appreciates the opportunity to provide input on Staff’s discussion draft regarding large
load interconnection standards introduced through SB6. The large load interconnection standards are
critical to get “right,” as the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) region faces
unprecedented load growth in the next five years, which will bring both challenges for the grid and
significant opportunities for business development in the state. In anticipation of this growth, the
Legislature set complimentary goals for the Commission to balance in implementing the large load
interconnection standards required by PURA § 37.0561—i.e., to both “support business development
in this state while [also] minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining
system reliability.” 4

        NRG generally supports the framework of the draft rule, which requires material and
meaningful financial commitment by large loads, while also setting achievable standards and providing
opportunities for refunds. NRG proposes some changes to the draft that are needed to fully achieve the
statutory aims. As proposed, the draft rule would require large loads to both fully fund the direct costs
associated with interconnecting the large load to the grid (i.e., the “driveway) through a contribution in
aid of construction (CIAC) (which NRG supports) and also fund (either alone or with other large loads)
certain system upgrades (i.e., the “highway”) that are “directly attributable” to the large load (which

NRG has concerns with). In addition to introducing unnecessary complexity to the rule (e.g.,
determining what is “directly attributable” to the large load or a group of large loads versus what
benefits the system as a whole), the proposal to require large loads to pay for costs that are typically
socialized to all loads would be a fundamental shift in the transmission cost recovery paradigm that
exists today in ERCOT. In addition, the justification for delaying refunds of the relatively high per
megawatt (MW) financial security—which NRG supports increasing (perhaps even doubling) to
achieve the critical goal of disciplining the queue—for as long as five years is questionable if large
loads are already required to fully fund (through a non-refundable CIAC) all system upgrades directly
attributable to their interconnection. Taken together, those provisions would be overly punitive,
contradicting the statutory directive for the standards to “support business development.” NRG thus
urges the Commission to focus on setting the refundable financial security high enough to discipline
the queue, while addressing the need for large loads to contribute to the ongoing cost of system upgrades
(as required by SB6) by reforming the four coincident peak (4CP) transmission cost allocation
methodology that is currently under consideration in Project No. 58484. In the large load
interconnection rule, the CIAC requirements should apply to the “driveway” only.

       In addition to this overarching comment, NRG proposes other modifications below that are
intended to improve the efficiency and timing of the large load interconnection process, along with
streamlining and clarifying the rule language. NRG also recommends that the rule provide for partial
refunds of the study fee in the event a large load withdraws from the interconnection process, as well
as incorporate an ability for large loads or project developers to expedite the process by providing
additional security or demonstrating that onsite generation at the site will address potential reliability
concerns.

                              COMMENTS ON DISCUSSION DRAFT

   1. Subsection (c) – Disclosures and study fee upon receipt of interconnection request

       a. Subsection (c)(4) - Schedule for phased energization of requested peak demand

       Proposed subsection (c)(4) would require the large load customer to provide an expected
monthly load ramp schedule as part of the initial disclosures that the large load must submit before the
interconnecting electric utility will begin the study process. At this early stage, a monthly ramp schedule
would not be possible to estimate with any degree of accuracy. Thus, NRG recommends that the rule
require only a quarterly schedule at this point, which could be updated to a monthly schedule later in
the process (i.e., during the intermediate phase contemplated by proposed section (h)).

         NRG’s proposed rule language is below:

         (4)        Schedule for phased energization of requested peak demand. A large load
                    customer must disclose to the interconnecting electric utility the expected

                    requested peak demand expressed in MW and megavolt-ampere reactive
                    (MVAr) units.

         b. Subsection (c)(5) - Backup generating facilities

         Proposed subsection (c)(5) pertains to the disclosures that SB6 requires regarding backup
generating facilities, the purpose of which is to ensure that ERCOT is able to direct the utilities to
require deployment of those facilities at a certain point during emergency grid conditions. 5 In order to
ensure that the disclosures are helpful to achieve that purpose, the draft rule should require that the
disclosures include any run hour limitations under any existing environmental permits for the facilities
and detail how quickly the facility can reach its full capability to serve the large load. With respect to
the former, environmental permit restrictions will be relevant to ERCOT to determine how many hours
a year ERCOT can anticipate that the facilities will be available to serve the large load during a grid
emergency; while that information might not be known at the start of the interconnection process, the
rule can clarify that the information sought is based on what is known at the time (e.g., by referencing
“existing” permits and “any” limitations), and later sections in the rule (subsections (e) and (h)) would
require updates to this information as applicable. With respect to the latter, the proposed rule would
require a disclosure regarding how quickly the backup facilities could turn on, but for ERCOT’s
purposes, it seems more relevant for ERCOT to know when the facilities could serve the load to their
full capability 6 and thus effectively remove that load from what the grid must serve during an applicable
emergency condition.

         c. Subsection (c)(7) - Study fee

         In its earlier comments in this project, NRG supported setting the study fee at the $100,000 level
set out in the statute, but is not opposed to the higher values proposed in the rule (i.e., $114,000 for
large loads with peak demand lower than 250 MW and $314,000 for large loads with peak demand of
250 MW or more), provided there is a mechanism to true up the study fee if the payment is too high or
low and that a refund mechanism is added for withdrawals.

         With respect to true ups, the draft rule already appropriately addresses the circumstance where
the study fee turns out to be too low, by requiring the large load customer to pay the excess. However,
the draft rule does not address the circumstance where the large load customer overpays. Under SB6,
if the study fee amount turns out to be too high, then any unused portion of the fee must be used as a
credit toward satisfying financial obligations for procurement or interconnection agreements at the
site. 7 NRG recommends language to incorporate this feature of SB6 into the draft rule in the redline
below.

         With respect to refunds for withdrawals, neither SB6 nor the draft rule appear to address what
happens with the study fee if the large load customer withdraws their interconnection request before
the study is completed (and before the interconnecting electric utility has incurred all the associated
costs). Both SB6 and the draft rule address refunds in the context of financial security, 8 and SB6
addresses overpayments of the study fee if the large load customer proceeds through the process (as
noted above). But there does not appear to be any guidance for the circumstance where the customer
withdraws early enough in the process that the interconnecting electric utility has not completed or
otherwise incurred the full cost of the study. In other markets (e.g., PJM), a partial refund is provided

to allow sufficient time for the large load customer or project developer to verify the change and gather
any associated details or documentation. Second, the timeline for the large load customer to pay an

      3. Subsection (e) – Discretionary Services Agreement

         a. Introduction paragraph to subsection (e) - General timing considerations

         In the introductory paragraph of subsection (e), NRG proposes clarifying that the reference to
the large load interconnection study that the utility will provide to ERCOT is to the “completed” study.
Further, the draft rule should clarify that the requirements in subsection (e) (including financial
commitment) can occur concurrently with providing the disclosures under subsection (c). While some
large load customers might want to await the results of the interconnection study before deciding
whether to complete the required steps in subsection (e) to move forward in the process, others may
wish to expedite the process by providing all required disclosures and financial security at the outset of
the study process.

         b. Subsection (e)(2) - Disclosure requirements related to site control

         With respect to site control, NRG appreciates the draft rule’s inclusion of “options” as a way to
demonstrate site control, as that is a common legal instrument used early in the development process
and is accepted in the generation interconnection context. 11 With that said, typically, an option is limited
in duration to a year or two into the development process, at which time the “option” is exercised and
converts to a lease or purchase agreement once the large load customer/project developer is more certain
that the project will proceed to energization. An option would unlikely extend through “50% of the
expected time to reach the peak demand” (as proposed in the draft rule), which could represent several
years and would not make sense once the load begins to energize (at which time the load would need a
legal right to occupy the land through an actual lease or purchase, not just an option). Thus, NRG
recommends that the site control, for purposes of subsection (e) of the draft rule, include an option up
to the execution of the intermediate agreement contemplated by subsection (h) of the draft rule (at
which time, the draft rule would already require something more than an option to demonstrate site
control – i.e., an executed lease or deed).

       c. Subsections (e)(4) – (5) - Disclosure requirements related to studies and regulatory
          approvals

       NRG proposes a few changes to subsections (e)(4) and (5) related to studies and regulatory
approvals, which are intended to strike a balance between requiring large load customers to provide
enough information to demonstrate they have a plan for necessary studies and regulatory approvals and
thus are “real,” without being unnecessarily burdensome by requiring too frequent of updates or an
exhaustive list of every required approval. In crafting the requirements for this subsection (and the rule
as a whole), the Commission should bear in mind the stated goals of PURA § 37.0561 to both support
business development (e.g., through not imposing overly burdensome requirements) while also
minimizing stranded costs (e.g., through ensuring that the large loads in the queue are “real”). To that
end, NRG recommends that the draft rule require updates to the large load customer’s plans for both
studies (subsection (e)(4)) and regulatory approvals (subsection (e)(5)) on no more than a quarterly
basis. In addition, the plan regarding state and local regulatory approvals should be limited to the types
of approvals that the regulatory authority has discretion to approve or deny (i.e., “discretionary”
permits) and should not include ministerial approvals (like building permits) that will be granted as a
matter of course. Further, some local approvals like building permits will not be planned years in
advance, as those are ministerial permits that can be sought much later in the process. The goal should
be to require the large load customer to demonstrate they have a general understanding and plan for the
major, material permits and studies that will be required to interconnect and operate. Finally, with
respect to the plan for required studies, NRG recommends adding a reference to “geotechnical survey”
as one of the major site-related studies that a large load customer should include in its plan.

        e. Subsection (e)(8) – Financial Security on a dollar per MW basis

        The dollar per MW financial security is one of the most critical parts of the draft rule that, if set
at the right value, should go a long way toward bringing discipline to the large load queue, which is

                         NRG ENERGY, INC.'S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   The proliferation of large loads will undoubtedly pose challenges and opportunities for the ERCOT
    market. Establishing interconnection standards is an important step in the evolution ofthe processes
    at ERCOT to accommodate this unprecedented growth.
•   In implementing this step of the Senate Bill 6 (SB6) implementation, NRG encourages the
    Commission to bear in mind the complimentary goals of PURA § 37.0561-i.e., "support business
    development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and
    maintaining system reliability"-and to set financial commitment requirements that are both
    meaningful and achievable.
•   The draft rule goes a long way toward meeting the statutory goals, but NRG has concerns that the
    proposal for large load customers to pay for system upgrades that are "directly attributable" to their
    interconnection is overly complex and could be overly punitive, especially if coupled with a
    relatively high dollar per megawatt (MW) financial security requirement that would be tied up for
    as long as five years after energization. [subsection (h)(9)(B)]
    o   The justification for a long delay for the refund seems to be incentivizing large loads to take
        service and operate long enough to contribute meaningfully to the recovery of transmission
        system costs (i.e., and to thus "minimiz[el the potential for stranded infrastructure costs" in line
        with PURA). However, if the load already must pay directly for system upgrades "directly
      attributable" to its interconnection, then the long refund period seems unnecessary and overly
      punitive.
    o NRG supports maintaining the "driveway" / "highway" split of costs that exists today for
      interconnecting entities and only requiring the CIAC to cover the driveway, while addressing
      the highway costs by reforming the four coincident peak (4CP) transmission cost allocation
        methodology as is currently under consideration in Project No. 58484.
•   The dollar per MW financial security amount could be set even higher (potentially double) the
    proposed $50,000 per MW amount, as this value is one of the most critical parts of the rule to help
    discipline the large load interconnection queue and allow the projects that are "real" and ready to
    move forward to do so more expeditiously. [subsection (e)(8)]
•   In addition, NRG proposes that large load customers be given the opportunity to expedite the
    procurement of transmission equipment and services by paying additional financial security or
    demonstrating that they will co-locate with generation behind-the-meter to address potential
    reliability issues (like ride through or resource adequacy). [subsection (h)(8)]
•   Additional changes that NRG proposes relate to timing elements in the rule - i.e., (1) providing a
    longer time to update disclosures to the utility (10 days instead of 5 days) and to post additional
    security when additional capacity is requested (30 days instead of 10 days) [subsection (d)(1)-(2)];
